title: The Building That Wasn't There
excerpt: Inspector Verel receives a call from an address that the city records insist is an empty lot.
content:
The call came in at 11:58, two minutes before the city stopped counting the night shift.

"There's a body at 44 Vesh Street," the dispatcher said, and Inspector Verel — six hours from the end of a double shift, three cups of cold coffee deep — wrote it down without thinking.

Then she thought about it.

Vesh Street ended at the freight elevators. There was no number 44. There was no number 40. There were, according to the municipal register she had personally signed off on in spring, eleven numbers on Vesh Street, and all of them were warehouses.

"44 Vesh," she repeated. "You're sure."

"I'm reading what the caller gave us. Do you want the address or not?"

She wanted the address. She wanted, more than she wanted sleep, to know who had called a dispatch line that was supposed to be outbound-only between eleven and dawn, and why the recording system — which never missed anything — had no audio from the call at all.

The taxi driver refused the fare at 43 Vesh. "Nothing past the freight yard," he said, not meeting her eyes. "Nothing's ever been past the freight yard."

He was wrong, of course. Inspector Verel could see the building from where he dropped her: a narrow tower of dark glass standing exactly where the empty lot should have been, tall enough that she had to tilt her head back to find its roof against the stars.

Every window was lit.

Every window was empty.

She stepped through the gate, and the streetlights behind her went out, one by one, in the order she had passed them.

## The Register

Inside, the lobby was marble and warm air and the low hum of a building running smoothly at midnight, which was itself the first wrong thing — freight yards sleep at midnight, and so does their marble.

A concierge desk. A concierge. A man in grey livery with a patient, professional face that did not match anything human about the moment.

"Inspector," he said, before she showed a badge. "Floor forty-four. You're expected."

She had not told anyone she was coming.

"Who's expecting me?"

The concierge's smile did not move, which was, she noticed, the second wrong thing: it had been exactly that wide since she walked in.

"The deceased, Inspector. Left instructions." He slid a brass key across the marble, and it chimed against the counter like a struck glass. "She said you'd want the register first."

The register was a ledger, leather-bound, older than the city. On the first line, in ink that hadn't faded, was Verel's own name — written in handwriting she recognized because she saw it every day in the mirror.
